newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish coalition split seen as electioneering.
newsitem.headline: Polish coalition split seen as electioneering.

text.p: Poland's co-ruling Peasant Party confirmed an ultimatum to the prime minister on Wednesday, just weeks away from a general election.

But opposition politicians said conflict within the leftist coalition was unlikely to bring down the government. The Peasants appeared to be jockeying for electoral advantage, in a row partly linked to catastrophic floods which killed 54 people last month.
The Peasant Party (PSL) has said it will try to dismiss Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz unless the cabinet grants advance payments to farmers for the grain harvest by next Tuesday.
PSL Agriculture Minister Jaroslaw Kalinowski ostentatiously walked out of a cabinet meeting on Tuesday when Cimoszewicz refused to discuss the proposed advances.
Opposition politicians said the PSL was taking a stand in order to boost its support among rural voters in the run-up to parliamentary elections on September 21.

"The Peasants can now distance themselves from the government and criticise some of its polices. It is easier to campaign from critical positions," said Tomasz Tywonek of the right-leaning opposition Solidarity alliance.

"We have seen similar conflicts in the coalition dozens of times. The parties will come to an agreement this time, too. The Peasants will probably get more or less what they want and score points in the electoral campaign," said Henryk Wujec, senior official of the opposition Union for Freedom party.

The Peasants and the opposition could theoretically muster the simple majority needed to dismiss Cimoszewicz in a parliamentary no-confidence vote, but Wujec said his party was unlikely to support such a move.
"There is no point in dismissing the prime minister just before the elections," he said.

The PSL could nevertheless obstruct the workings of the government to press for his dismissal. Its leadership held a crisis session on Tuesday and confirmed its ultimatum after a further meeting on Wednesday.
"Our standpoint is final," Peasant parliamentary deputy Stanislaw Kalemba told Reuters.
Cimoszewicz's ex-communist party, the Democratic Left Alliance which is the senior partner in the coalition, made conciliatory noises and played down the conflict.
"I think that Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz will finds ways to liquidate these tensions," PAP news agency quoted ex-communist leader Jozef Oleksy as saying.

Government spokeswoman Aleksandra Jakubowska said late on Tuesday that the cabinet would discuss the advances for farmers as soon as the agriculture minister presents a detailed report on the food market after catastrophic floods throughout July.

Kalinowski wants the government to authorise the Agriculture Market Agency (ARR), the food market regulator, to borrow 120 million zlotys ($35 million) to begin granting the advances to farmers. The ARR's funds have been depleted by aid payments it made to farmers hit by the floods.
The Peasants, in power with the ex-communists since 1993, have suggested that after the elections they may form a new coalition with Solidarity.
